newsitem.title: USA: Bulgaria merits upgrade to B1 - Merrill Lynch.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria merits upgrade to B1 - Merrill Lynch.

text.p: NEW YORK, July 31 - Bulgaria's creditworthiness has improved dramatically in the past six months and is currently out of date, according to Merrill Lynch fixed income strategist, Andrew Kenningham.

In a press release, Kenningham said, major U.S. credit rating agencies are likely to award Bulgaria, who currently holds the lowest credit rating of any sovereign borrower at B3, a B1 rating by early 1998.
The strategist added that if current favorable economic and political trends continue Bulgaria could conceivably be upgraded to a low BB range by 1999.
He noted, Bulgaria's political environment which has improved since the election on April 19 of a pro-reform government, which holds a parliamentary majority.

Inaddition to, Bulgaria's economic outlook, which has been transformed by the implementation of an IMF backed stabilization program, which is anchored by a currency board that introduced on July, 1, with an exhange rate peg of BGL1000/DEM.

Risk of debt default which existed this year, has been addressed by the privatisation programme, increased official loans from the IMF and World Bank, and improved health of the banking secto, according to the Merrill Lynch strategist.

"Total returns for Bulgarian Brady bonds have exceeded 50 percent since the beginning of the year, due to the radical fall in default risk, making these bonds by the top performing asset in the Brady market this year," Kenningham said.
Bulgarian Brady bonds are expected to continue providing attractive, though more modest returns, over the next 18 months, Kenningham said.

"We believe that the 12-month lev Treasury bills also look attractive at 5.4 percent over Deutschemark interest rates since the risk of a devaluation is extremely low over this time horizon," he said.

Kenningham predicted inflation will fall to around 12 percent in 1998; and noted that interest rates falling dramatically since March will result in a drop in interest payments on domestic debt, to 2.5 percent of GDP in 1998, compared to 18 percent in 1996.

Bulgaria's fiscal deficit is expected to fall to only 1.0 percent of GDP in 1998, compared to 11 percent in 1996; the economy is expected to rebound in 1998, with GDP growth of about four percent, compared to a projected seven percent contraction in growth for the '97 year.
The country's foreign exchange reserves are expected to reach US$1.9 billion by year-end compared to only US$520 million at end-1996, according to Kenningham.
